newsitem.title: USA: China warns against too high WTO "admission fee".
newsitem.headline: China warns against too high WTO "admission fee".

text.p: China is ready to make economic reforms in order to join the World Trade Organisation but if the admission fee "is too high, then we cannot afford it," Trade Minister Wu Yi said on Friday.

"We are prepared to show greater flexibility" in upcoming negotiations over acceptance into the global trade body, she said. Acceptance would assure a market for China's rapidly growing export industry.

Wu told a news conference China should be admitted to the WTO under the more lenient rules given to developing nations. U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said China should meet a stricter standard, taking into account its huge economy.

The trade ministers sparred over a Chinese rule that effectively has cut off U.S. wheat sales. Kantor said the rule might be a disguised trade barrier. Wu offered to quit her job if anyone could prove China was applying different rules to other grain exporters.
U.S. and Chinese officials have disagreed for months over terms for China's entry into the WTO.

On Wednesday, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshevsky said China was "treading water" rather than taking steps that would allow its entry. U.S. officials say China should undertake reforms opening its markets to imported goods.

Wu said Chinese entry to WTO "must be in line with our economic development," adding: "If the request for our admission fee is too high, we cannot afford it. I do not have so much money in my pocket."

She said China had no timetable for joining the trade body and noted 10 years have passed since it said it wanted to join. "Whether or when China joins the WTO, China will not stop its reforms and its opening-up policy," she said.

The United States has said it would support China as a member if adequate changes are made in its economy. For instance, U.S. officials have said China should rein in government trading enterprises that enjoy monopoly control over exports and imports of many goods.
Barshevsky said on Wednesday there had been no real movement in China's position in two years.

China is the fifth larges U.S. trade partner and stands second to Japan in the size of its trade surplus. The U.S. trade deficit with China hit $34 billion in 1995 and neared $20 million in the first seven months of this year.

Wu used strong language in defending China's policy of rejecting any wheat that might contain TCK smut, a fungus, saying "maybe we were taken in" when China inadverently imported 1 million metric tons of TCK-tainted wheat this year.
Kantor said China "imports TCK wheat from Canada but not from the United States." Wu said if anyone could prove that charge, "I will give up my post ..."

U.S. officials say China's policy is unfair and TCK smut poses no threat to China's grain-growing regions. More than 1 million tonnes of U.S. wheat sales to China were cancelled this year as the dispute flared.

At the end of two days of talks, U.S. and Chinese officials announced three contracts for U.S. firms to sell software to Chinese agencies and $495 million in loan guarantees to sell four Boeing 777 aircraft and three McDonnell-Douglas MD-90 aircraft to two Chinese airlines.
